questions.knowledge_point: Line Integrals Over Circles and Ellipses
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14069622/assets/dea7eed9213ddf1bb3293950e2490b120a061e9add1172d3b850ccbc58f90454.png)

Evaluate the line integral ${\int }_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=(y+x)\,i+x\,j$ and $C$ is the arc of the ellipse ${x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}=4$ traversed from the point $A(-2,0)$ to the point $B(0,-1).$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the curve. Notice that we can write its equation as

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+{y}^{2}=1.
$$

So, our curve is a part-ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $2$ and $1$ respectively. This curve can be parameterized as

$$
r(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,\pi \le t\le \frac{3\pi }{2}.
$$

So, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =(y+x)\,i+x\,j \\  & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =((\operatorname{sin}⁡t+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j)\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2(-{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t) \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t+2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t+2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)\,dt \\  & =[\operatorname{cos}⁡2t+\operatorname{sin}⁡2t]_{\pi }^{3\pi /2} \\  & =[-1+0]-[1-0] \\  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14069622/assets/08c3195e7325d853f61562b1f62460cb0796f14377286228f2b7cd40983202ac.png)

Evaluate the line integral ${\int }_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=3\,i+\frac{1}{x}\,j$ and $C$ is the arc of the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=16$  traversed from the point $A(4,0)$ to the point $B(0,4).$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize a circle of radius $4$ centered at the origin. It can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le \frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

So, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=4\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

As a result,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =3\,i+\frac{1}{x}\,j \\  & =3\,i+\frac{1}{4\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(3\,i+\frac{1}{4\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,j)\cdot (-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =3\cdot (-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+\frac{1}{4\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\cdot 4\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-12\operatorname{sin}⁡t+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(-12\operatorname{sin}⁡t+1)\,dt \\  & =[12\operatorname{cos}⁡t+t]_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =(0+\frac{\pi }{2})-(12+0) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}-12\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)\,i+\sqrt{xy}\,j$ and $C$ is the line segment traversed from the point $A(1,1)$ to the point $B(4,3)?$

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=(1+3t)\,i+(1+2t)\,j.$*
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the line segment.
The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are 
$a=i+j$ and $b=4\,i+3\,j.$
So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t(b-a) \\  & =(i+j)+t[(4\,i+3\,j)-(i+j)] \\  & =(i+j)+t(3i+2\,j) \\  & =(1+3t)\,i+(1+2t)\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t$ varies from $t=0$ (at the point $A$) to $t=1$ (at the point $B$).
Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=1+3t,\,y=1+2t.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)\,i+\sqrt{xy}\,j \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+3t+1+2t)\,i+\sqrt{(1+3t)(1+2t)}\,j \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+5t)\,i+\sqrt{1+5t+6{t}^{2}}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+3t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+2t)j \\  & =3\,i+2\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+5t)\,i+\sqrt{1+5t+6{t}^{2}}\,j)\cdot (3\,i+2\,j) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+5t)\cdot 3+\sqrt{1+5t+6{t}^{2}}\cdot 2 \\  & =3\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+5t)+2\sqrt{1+5t+6{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}3\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+5t)+2\sqrt{1+5t+6{t}^{2}}\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Evaluate ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=x\,i+2y\,j$ and $C$ is the curve $\operatorname{ln}⁡y-x=0$ traversed from the point $A(0,1)$ to the point $B(1,e).$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the curve. Making $x$ the subject of the equation, we have

$$
\operatorname{ln}⁡y-x=0\,⟹\,x=\operatorname{ln}⁡y.
$$

So, the parametrization of the curve is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡t\,i+t\,j,\,1\le t\le e.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{ln}⁡t,\,y=t.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =x\,i+2y\,j \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡t\,i+2t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =\frac{1}{t}\,i+j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡t\,i+2t\,j)\cdot (\frac{1}{t}\,i+j) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡t\cdot \frac{1}{t}+2t\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡t}{t}+2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{1}^{e}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{e}(\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡t}{t}+2t)\,dt \\  & ={[\frac{{ln}^{2}⁡t}{2}+{t}^{2}]}_{1}^{e} \\  & =(\frac{{ln}^{2}⁡e}{2}+{e}^{2})-(0+1) \\  & ={e}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=2y\,i+{x}^{2}\,j$ and $C$ is the curve $\sqrt{y}=x+3$ traversed from the point $A(-3,0)$ to the point $B(-1,4)?$

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=(\sqrt{t}-3)\,i+t\,j.$*
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the curve. This is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =(\sqrt{t}-3)\,i+t\,j,\,0\le t\le 4.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\sqrt{t}-3,\,y=t.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =2t\,i+(\sqrt{t}-3)^{2}\,j \\  & =2t\,i+(t-6\sqrt{t}+9)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{t}-3)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}\,i+j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(2t\,i+(t-6\sqrt{t}+9)\,j)\cdot (\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}\,i+j) \\  & =2t\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}+t-6\sqrt{t}+9 \\  & =\sqrt{t}+t-6\sqrt{t}+9 \\  & =t-5\sqrt{t}+9.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{4}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}(t-5\sqrt{t}+9)\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$
